ki-27_otsu: Nakajima's Type 97 Fighter of 1937 was the Japanese Army's first monoplane fighter, and 3,368 were built before the Ki-43 took over its frontline role in 1942. In the game it lives at low level: below about 1,000 m few comparable fighters can stay with it in a turn. Only two 7.7 mm guns and thin protection make it a weak interceptor, so it is better suited to covering friendly bombers and flying boats than to chasing targets down. It arrived in Update 1.43.
ki-27_otsu_china: Nakajima's Ki-27 (Allied codename "Nate") ended up with both sides of China's armed forces; the Nationalists found little use for it as a fighter, while the Communists put captured examples to work training pilots and engineers. Its flight model matches the Japanese version, so it turns superbly, but anything with a stronger engine or a height advantage is a real danger. It does best against enemies already dragged down low, either finishing them or crippling them for an assist. It came with the Chinese tree in Update 1.91 "Night Vision".
ki-27_otsu_ep: A Ki-27 otsu in the colours of the 4th Sentai at Tachiarai Air Base in Fukuoka, Kyūshū, a site that became an Army flight school in 1940 and prepared new Army pilots for combat over Asia. It sums up the Japanese air tree's priorities: superb manoeuvrability comes first, while protection is middling and the guns are underwhelming. It was added in the "Starfighters" update.
ki-45_hei: The third production model of the Ki-45 two-seat fighter went back to a 20 mm belly cannon after the disappointing Otsu and swapped the twin nose 12.7 mm guns for a drum-fed 37 mm Ho-203, settling the type's role as a bomber interceptor able to climb to their altitude. Its combined 20 mm and 37 mm burst is the hardest-hitting of the Ki-45 family, and it handles much like the cannon-armed Kai-Kō. The 37 mm empties quickly, though, so short, deliberate bursts matter. It was introduced in Update 1.31.
ki-45_hei_tei_china: Assembled from three captured Ki-45s of the Hei and Tei variants, this single aircraft was rebuilt by Communist forces in north-eastern China after WWII for evaluation and instruction, and never served as a real combatant; the Chinese simply called it a "heavy fighter". It pairs the Hei's fuselage 20 mm Ho-3 with the Tei's two upward-firing 20 mm Ho-5s, so no other Ki-45 in the game carries as much firepower, though it has no ordnance. Agile for a twin-engined fighter, it is a strong bomber hunter, but its small ammunition supply leaves it struggling against fighters. It arrived in Update 1.93 "Shark Attack" as a Golden Eagles purchase.
ki-45_ko: The Kai-Kō was the first production Ki-45, a twin-seat, general-purpose fighter Kawasaki developed alongside the Ki-43 and Ki-44; early prototypes with Ha-25 engines lacked power, so the "Kai" re-engined it with Ha-102s. Armed with two nose 12.7 mm guns and a ventral 20 mm cannon, it carries the most forward-firing ammunition of any Ki-45. It is built for boom-and-zoom: climb and roll rate are only average, so gentle climbs and fast diving passes work better than turning. It came in Update 1.31.
ki-45_otsu: For the Kai-Otsu, the Ki-45's 20 mm cannon gave way to a Type 94 37 mm tank gun, the same weapon as the Ha-Go's, which the rear crewman had to reload by hand one round at a time. That makes it the awkward member of the family: the 37 mm carries little ammunition, fires slowly and drops sharply thanks to its short barrel, and even its APHE round penetrates poorly. In practice it flies like a heavy-cannon attacker without the big gun's payoff. It was introduced in Update 1.31.
ki-45_tei: The last Ki-45 production model borrowed the Navy J1N's idea of oblique Schräge Musik cannons, fitting two upward-firing 20 mm Ho-5s in place of the belly gun; production Tei aircraft also deleted the rear gunner. The in-game model is really a Kai-Hei with Tei armament, so the gunner remains. Firing the oblique guns needs a separate view keybind, and the method is to slide in beneath a bomber at matched speed and shoot from outside its gunners' arcs. Uniquely among Ki-45s, it can also carry ordnance, two 250 kg bombs. It arrived in Update 1.31.
ki-49_1: The Ki-49-I, the opening model of this Japanese bomber family in War Thunder, has been in the game since the open beta ahead of Update 1.27. It is quick in level flight, well protected from behind and, thanks to very large elevators, more agile than its size suggests; it was also the first Japanese bomber with substantial armour. That makes it flexible in air battles, able to bomb from low level or hit bases, and its speed means frequent trips to rearm can make up for a modest payload.
ki-49_2a: Japan's Ki-49 medium bomber was designed after Ki-21 operations showed that unescorted daylight raids needed far more armour and defensive guns; the IIa added stronger Ha-109 engines in place of the Ha-41s, self-sealing tanks and better armour. In the game it is a low-level attacker of pillboxes, tanks and similar ground targets, held back by a small bomb load but unusually nimble for a bomber. Its armour and guns, the dorsal 20 mm cannon above all, help drive off fighters. It has been in the game since the open beta, before Update 1.27.
ki-49_2b: A Japanese medium bomber in the game since the open beta (before Update 1.27), the Ki-49-IIb works best low down against pillboxes, tanks and other ground targets. Its total bomb load is small, but it turns well enough to circle over a target area and unload quickly, something big bombers such as the G8N1 Renzan struggle with. The 4 x 250 kg option suits tanks, pillboxes, bases and small ships.
ki-49_2b_late: Another Japanese bomber present since the open beta before Update 1.27, the Ki-49-IIb/L is meant for low-level strikes on ground targets such as tanks, pillboxes and small ships. It cannot carry much in total, but it is agile for its class and can keep circling over a target to drop everything in quick succession, unlike large, slow-turning heavies such as the G8N1. Against tanks, pillboxes or light ships, the four 250 kg bomb load is the recommended choice.
ki-83: Tomio Kubo's team, creators of the Ki-46, designed the Ki-83 to a 1943 Army requirement for a long-range heavy fighter, using two turbocharged 2,200 hp engines; in testing it reached 9,750 m in under ten minutes. Four prototypes flew, bombing raids stalled the programme, and the last survivor went to the US and was probably scrapped. In the game no propeller-driven aircraft out-climbs it; it also handles well and packs two 30 mm and two 20 mm nose cannons with plenty of ammunition. Its two 50 kg bombs are not worth the performance cost. It arrived in Update 1.57 "Battle March".
ki-96: Kawasaki built the Ki-96 privately in 1942 as a bigger-engined follow-on to its Ki-45; the Army asked for it as a single-seater, then went back to wanting two seats and cancelled it, though its wings and tail lived on in the Ki-102. The game's version follows the later single-seat prototypes, armed with a 37 mm Ho-203 and two 20 mm Ho-5s in the nose. It shreds bombers from oblique angles, suits boom-and-zoom, and is nimble enough to dogfight single-engined fighters, but ammunition runs short quickly. It was added in Update 1.35.
ki_100_2: Kawasaki began the Ki-100-II in March 1945 as a high-altitude interceptor against B-29 formations, giving its Ha-112-II Ru engine a turbocharger and water-methanol injection; only three prototypes were completed before Japan's defeat. Compared with the standard Ki-100 it gives up speed and agility at low and medium heights in exchange for strong performance at 8–10 km, where few fights take place. Even so, it stays well rounded, and its nose armament is heavy by Japanese standards, enough for both fighters and four-engined bombers. It came in Update 1.65 "Way of the Samurai".
ki_100_early: Developed from the Ki-61-II by fitting a Ha-112-2 radial, the Ki-100 climbed faster and let Japan contest Allied raids on the home islands in 1945. Its default camouflage carries the markings of the 59th Sentai, a unit that fought in China and then from Java to New Guinea before returning to defend northern Kyushu, ending the war on Ki-100s. In the game it carries over the Ki-61's all-round balance of speed, dive, climb, turning and firepower: nothing stands out, but it gives the pilot plenty of ways to fight. It was introduced in Update 1.61 "Road to Glory".
ki_102_otsu: Known informally as the Type 4 Assault Aircraft, the Ki-102 otsu was a twin-engined, two-seat attacker derived from the Ki-45 that entered service in 1944; it saw little action beyond Okinawa and was mostly held back for home defence. It carries a 57 mm nose cannon, two ventral 20 mm cannons and a rear 12.7 mm gun. It can work as a ground attacker against light and soft targets or as an improvised bomber hunter; the 57 mm hits hard but is inaccurate, so single shots work better than bursts. It arrived in Update 1.35.
ki_108: Derived from the Ki-96 and Ki-102, the Ki-108 Kai was a heavy fighter prototype with a pressurised cockpit, meant to reach B-29s at altitude on turbosupercharged Ha-112-II Ru radials; just four were built and none fought. In the game it pairs a 37 mm nose cannon and two 20 mm chin guns with solid climb and fair agility, but its engines are easily knocked out. It is best used on bombers, attacking head-on or from the flank to stay clear of their gunners, and should avoid even fights with fighters, as it can neither out-turn nor outrun them. It was added in Update 1.77 "Advancing Storm".
ki_109: Mitsubishi's Ki-67 bomber was converted into the Ki-109 interceptor to counter the US high-altitude raids on Japan, gaining an adapted 75 mm anti-aircraft gun and losing every defensive position except the tail turret. The big gun can bring down bombers and, with a clean hit, knock out tanks, but it is no tool for agile fighters or other fast-moving targets. With such weak defensive fire, fighters are best avoided altogether. It joined the game in Update 1.71 "New E.R.A.".
ki_10_1: Takeo Doi, Richard Vogt's successor as Kawasaki's chief designer, drew up the Ki-10, a V-12-powered biplane that beat Nakajima's monoplane Ki-11 for an Army contract because it turned better. Entering service in 1937, it fought in China and South-east Asia and was the Army's last biplane fighter. In the game it is swifter than rival biplanes and gains height more easily, yet it is lightly armed and poorly protected, with two slow-firing 7.7 mm guns best loaded with stealth belts. Its place is low-level turning fights with biplanes and slow monoplanes, aiming at wings and leaving bombers alone. It has been in the game since the open beta.
ki_10_1_commander: A Ki-10-I in the markings of the 1st Hiko Sentai, the Japanese Army Air Service's first flying unit, formed on 5 July 1938; it flew the type until May 1942 before converting to the Ki-27, after which the Ki-10 went to training and secondary roles. Performance matches the other Ki-10s: good turning, reasonable climb and low speed, with little armour and light 7.7 mm armament that is outclassed against bombers or armoured aircraft. It does best turning with biplanes and slow monoplanes at low altitude, with team support. It has been in the game since the open beta.
ki_10_2: Kawasaki's Ki-10-II improved on the first model by fitting a more powerful engine under a redesigned cowling, plus an enlarged rudder and reinforced undercarriage, lifting top speed from 400 to 430 km/h and climb from 11.7 to 13.3 m/s. In the game it plays almost like the Ki-10-I: a good low-altitude turner with more speed and climb than rival biplanes, but with flimsy protection and two slow-firing 7.7 mm guns, for which stealth belts are the pick. Its prey is other biplanes and slow monoplanes; armoured targets and bombers are best left to others. It has been available since the open beta.
ki_10_2_commander: Painted for the 77th Hiko Sentai, formed in July 1938 out of the 8th Daitai, this Ki-10-II wears the unit's coloured tail field with thin stripes and twin "seagull" arrowheads that read as "77". The unit supported ground offensives in China and kept flying Ki-10s even after Soviet-supplied I-15s and I-16s outclassed them. It handles like the standard Ki-10-II, turning well at low level with weak guns and little armour. It has been in the game since the open beta but can no longer be obtained; only players who got it before its removal still have it.
ki_21_1hei: The Ki-21-Ic, third production version of the Type 97 Heavy Bomber, kept the Ib's revised control surfaces and added extra machine guns and bigger fuel tanks for range. It looks like any other Ki-21, but its defensive firepower is three times greater, with two more guns on each side and a remotely operated tail gun that punishes fighters sitting directly behind. It first appeared in Update 1.65 "Way of the Samurai" as a 2016 Winter Holiday event reward, and was later a Warbond battle trophy from Battle Pass Season I to Season IV.
ki_21_1ko: The Ki-21, or Type 97 Heavy Bomber, was designed around speed and range rather than armour or payload, the idea being to hit enemy airfields before their fighters could take off and to outrun interceptors; the Ia was its first production model, and it lost effectiveness as the war went on. In the game it is a nimble low-level bomber with a small total load, good against pillboxes, tanks, destroyers and cargo ships. Twenty 50 kg bombs suit scattered ground targets and two 500 kg bombs suit bases, while the light turrets favour higher altitudes. It arrived in Update 1.49 "Weapons of Victory".
ki_32: Designed in 1936 to replace the Kawasaki Ki-3, the Ki-32 light bomber was required to reach 400 km/h, carry 450 kg of bombs and dive at 60 degrees; 854 were produced up to 1940, and it left frontline service in December 1941. It opens the Japanese dive-bomber line, and its high-altitude spawn lets it reach bases before fighters can climb to it despite a low top speed. It turns well enough to hold its own against contemporary monoplanes with its single wing gun, while twin rear 7.7 mm guns give solid protection from low-rank attackers. It was added in Update 1.79 "Project X".
ki_43_1: First production model of Nakajima's Hayabusa, the Ki-43-I grew out of the Ki-27 with more speed and climb in mind; it first flew on 12 December 1938, but poor pilot feedback delayed adoption until early 1941, and roughly 750 were built in 1941–42 before the Ki-43-II took over. While the Navy's Zero took the headlines, the Hayabusa carried much of the Army's air war. In the game it shows the typical Japanese trade-off: outstanding agility, paid for with low top speed and poor survivability, and few aircraft are better at close turning fights. It was introduced in Update 1.43.
ki_43_2: Nakajima reworked the Ki-43 in 1942 to fix its fragile wing, low speed and inability to carry bombs: the Ki-43-II got a stronger Ha-115 engine, a three-bladed propeller, a reinforced wing with racks for bombs or drop tanks, a pilot backplate and protected fuel tanks. About 5,000 were built and served across the Pacific. In the game the gains are modest but meaningful: slightly higher speed, a wing that tolerates hard manoeuvres at almost any speed, and two bombs for mixed battles, all while remaining one of the most agile aircraft around. It has been in the game since the open beta.
ki_43_3_ko: Chinese forces captured Ki-43s (Allied codename "Oscar") more than once: a Ki-43-Ic was taken in April 1942, the Nationalist air force flew surviving examples around Nanjing until 1946, and the Communists turned eight into trainers. This Ki-43-III ko has an uprated engine for better diving speed. Its two 12.7 mm nose guns remain a weak armament, but the airframe keeps the Hayabusa's superb agility, even against Japanese opponents. It joined the game with the Chinese tech tree in Update 1.91 "Night Vision".
ki_43_3_otsu: A Japanese Army Hayabusa variant, the Ki-43-III otsu is light and extremely agile, with excellent climb and roll rates, but fragile enough that even rifle-calibre hits can do real harm. Its key change from the Ki-43-II is armament: two 20 mm Ho-5 cannons replace the 12.7 mm Ho-103s, giving it the punch to destroy most opponents. With just 300 rounds, short bursts from 200–500 m are the way to use them, and careful use of combat flaps and throttle lets it win most low and mid-altitude turning fights. It arrived in Update 1.45 "Steel Generals".
ki_44_1: Nakajima designed the Ki-44 alongside the light Ki-43 and twin-engined Ki-45 as a faster, cannon-armed answer to fighters like the Bf 109 and Spitfire; it ended up lighter than a Bf 109 and in some respects bettered an imported Bf 109 E-7, though visibility was poor and landing speed high. Service began in 1941, yet many experienced pilots resented giving up agility for speed. In the game it is still reasonably nimble, yet less so than the Ki-43 or A6M, so it works best diving on targets and climbing away to repeat the attack.
ki_44_1_ep: Ki-44-I 'Red 34' flew with the 47th Sentai, which began as the independent 47th Chutai, the first unit to receive the Ki-44; recalled from Indochina after the 1942 Doolittle Raid, it became a Sentai in 1943 and defended the homeland from Narimasu against B-29s, later adding a ramming "Shinten" flight and some Ki-84s. In the game the Ki-44 can finally trade blows with Western fighters on armament and mobility. It cannot turn with the Ki-43 or A6M, so boom-and-zoom suits it, but it is faster than those Japanese stablemates. It came in the "Starfighters" update.
ki_44_2_hei: The final standard Ki-44 model and the most produced, the IIc carried four 12.7 mm guns and a Type 100 optical sight, and many earlier aircraft were upgraded to match. Disliked by many pilots and overtaken by the Ki-84, it ended up mainly defending the home islands. The default scheme is that of the 70th Sentai, a B-29 interceptor unit whose pilots were readying for the Ki-200 when the war ended. In the game its four HE-loaded 12.7 mm guns hit hard, but opponents are tougher too, so it relies on a height advantage and quick kills before enemies can run it down. It arrived in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour".
ki_44_2_hei_china: China's Ki-44-II hei flies exactly like the Japanese original and arrived with Update 1.91 "Night Vision". The "Shoki" name refers to Zhong Kui, a powerful demon king of Chinese mythology known for his ugliness, which suits a squat, stubby fighter wearing weathered paint in Chinese service. Looks aside, it has outstanding performance for its rank, built around speed and climb while keeping good agility by non-Japanese standards, and pilots who know the CW-21 will find its tactics familiar.
ki_44_2_otsu: The Ki-44-IIb paired an improved engine and nose 12.7 mm guns with optional 40 mm wing cannons meant for American bombers, though they only worked at near-ramming range with little ammunition, and some were swapped for 12.7 mm guns; that close-in approach later fed into the Army's Shinten ramming units. In the game the 40 mm shells are devastating but painfully slow, so they are best saved for bombers and delivered from close range at speed; the strong engine gets it to altitude quickly. Once they are gone, the HE-loaded 12.7 mm guns make it a capable boom-and-zoom fighter. It arrived in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour".
ki_48_2_otsu: In the invasion of China, Japan's Ki-48 light bomber went after supply lines and infrastructure early in the war, and its crews valued the speed that let it outrun fighters. This Ki-48-II otsu was a gift reward from the 2023 Tokushu Heiki event, added in the "Sons of Attila" update, and it is the only propeller aircraft in the game able to carry a guided missile: the Ki-148, whose 130 kg TNT warhead wrecks the lightly armoured tanks it meets. Speed lets it get out of trouble, and two rear gunners discourage pursuers.
ki_61_1a_hei: Kawasaki's Ki-61-I hei, built from September 1943 to July 1944 alongside the otsu, replaced the wing machine guns with imported German MG 151/20 cannons, a stopgap while Japan's own 20 mm guns lagged; Kawasaki staff nicknamed it "Type Ma" after Mauser. The extra weight cost some performance. In the game it is the best-armed Ki-61-I, and the two 20 mm cannons kill fighters and bombers far more reliably than the kō and otsu's machine guns. It keeps the family's stability, strong dive and decent mid-altitude speed, and suits energy tactics and short, decisive engagements. It has been in the game since the open beta.
ki_61_1a_hei_ep: Takeichi Tada of the 78th Sentai flew this Ki-61-I hei. Formed in Manchuria in 1942 on Ki-27s, the unit converted to the Ki-61 in Japan, went to Rabaul in June 1943, scored the type's first aerial victory and was effectively wiped out by July 1944. In the game it turns well but is barely faster than early Zeros, though it accelerates and holds energy nicely, rather like a Bf 109 G-6. Its MG 151s with Minengeschoß shells and HE-loaded 12.7 mm guns are lethal, effective flaps help force overshoots, and it can carry bombs, of which 250 kg is the best choice. It came in the "Starfighters" update.
ki_61_1a_ko: Takeo Doi designed the Ki-61 to a 1940 Army requirement, building it around a licence-built DB 601 (Ha-40) with a sturdy metal airframe, self-sealing tanks and armour, and favouring hit-and-run tactics; it became Japan's only mass-produced fighter with a liquid-cooled inline engine. The first model, the kō, mixed two 12.7 mm and two 7.7 mm guns because heavy guns were in short supply, and unreliable engines dogged its service from 1943. In the game it is balanced rather than ultra-agile, faster than most Japanese contemporaries but average by other nations' standards, and the 7.7 mm guns mainly a fallback. It has been in the game since the open beta.
ki_61_1a_otsu: The second Ki-61 production model, built from September 1943 to April 1944, got the armament originally planned: four 12.7 mm Ho-103s, with the wing 7.7 mm guns gone. Lessons from the kō also brought better-protected fuel and extra armour for the pilot, and the tailwheel was fixed to ease production. In the game it keeps the Ki-61's balance of speed, stable mid-altitude handling and durability, while the four heavy machine guns give steadier hitting power than its predecessor. Climb and turn are not its strengths, so it works best as an energy fighter that picks its moments. It has been in the game since the open beta.
ki_61_1a_otsu_china: Flown in Chinese colours, this Ki-61-I otsu arrived in Update 1.91 "Night Vision". Compared with the Zero, the Ki-61 is faster, climbs better and handles better at speed, though it is less agile; its inline engine and gun layout give it a Bf 109-like look. In the game its climb is better than the stat card suggests, letting it reach heights few opponents can match and choose its fights, diving in and zooming away rather than turning. Its four 12.7 mm Ho-103s carry plenty of ammunition but lack punch and velocity, so close range and good lead are essential.
ki_61_1a_otsu_usa: An American-captured example of the Ki-61-I otsu, this premium has been in the game since the open beta. Like the Japanese version it carries four 12.7 mm Ho-103 guns with ample ammunition, and it outpaces, out-climbs and outguns the earlier Ki-43. Its real asset is climb, which is stronger than the stat card implies and lets it sit above most opponents and decide when to engage. It plays as an energy fighter: dive on a target, and if it survives, zoom back up out of reach of its guns for another pass.
ki_61_1a_tei: When imported MG 151 cannons ran out, the Ki-61-I tei (built January 1944 to January 1945) switched to two domestic 20 mm Ho-5s in the nose, which needed a longer nose, wings moved forward, rear ballast and a smaller main tank, and cost even more performance. Ha-140 engine delays kept it in production, making it the most numerous Ki-61. In the game it is a touch heavier and less agile than earlier Ki-61s, but the centreline cannons are accurate and free of convergence worries. It is best flown as an energy fighter, diving in for a decisive burst and extending away. It was introduced in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour".
ki_61_2_early: The Ki-61-II Kai was meant to cap the Ki-61 line with the DB 605-derived Ha-140, but the engine was so unreliable that many finished airframes sat engineless until they became Ki-100s. Its armament followed the Ki-61-I tei, with 12.7 mm guns kept in the wings, and later aircraft gained a teardrop canopy, which is why historians split the type into kō and otsu. In the game reliability is no issue, yet added weight eats most of the extra power, leaving it only slightly better than the tei; the real gain is 200 rounds per Ho-5 cannon instead of 120. It came in Update 1.59 "Flaming Arrows".
ki_67_1_ko: Designed to replace the Ki-49, the Ki-67 was built to survive, with armour and self-sealing tanks, while remaining agile enough to dive-bomb; it reached units in October 1944 and spawned variants such as the Ki-109 interceptor, but only 767 were completed. The Ko is the main production model with a single tail gun. In the game it is fast, tough and well defended, carries a wide choice of bombs and torpedoes, and is at its best attacking pillboxes and other individual ground targets rather than bases. It arrived in Update 1.67 "Assault".
ki_67_1_otsu: The Ki-67-I otsu is the later main production model of the Type 4 Heavy Bomber, which was intended to succeed the Ki-49 and combined armour and sealed tanks with enough agility for dive attacks; 767 Ki-67s of all versions were finished amid Allied raids. Its distinguishing feature is a twin-gun tail position, giving it stronger rear defence than the Ko. In the game it is quick and hard to bring down, with bombs or torpedoes for almost any role, though its load is better spent on pillboxes and other frontline targets than on bases. It joined the game in Update 1.67 "Assault".
ki_84_hei: Nakajima built the Ki-84 to succeed its Ki-43, keeping the agility while adding armour, heavier guns and better climb; it flew in April 1943, entered mass production in April 1944, and 3,514 of all versions were made. The Hei paired two 30 mm Ho-155s with two 20 mm Ho-5s. In the game it keeps the climb, smooth handling and agility of earlier Ki-84s, but it stiffens up at high speed, the heavy guns are hard to use well, and it turns worse than other Japanese fighters. Against tougher opposition its edge is smaller than its predecessors'. It was added in Update 1.37.
ki_84_ko: Nakajima's Ki-84 was ordered in 1942 to replace the Ki-43, fixing its weak guns, thin protection and climb with a pilot backplate, armoured glass, heavy machine guns and two 20 mm cannons. It first flew in April 1943, and the Ko, the first and most numerous production model, entered mass production in April 1944; 3,514 Ki-84s of all kinds were built, some ending up in China. In the game it climbs superbly and handles well, but its controls stiffen at high speed, its armament is light and other Japanese fighters out-turn it. It was introduced in Update 1.37.
ki_84_ko_china: Known as Hayate ("Gale") in Japanese service and "Frank" to the Allies, the Ki-84 first saw combat over mainland China defending Japanese assets from US and Nationalist bombers; after the 1945 surrender the Nationalist air force took over scattered examples until American aircraft arrived, while the Communists used them for ground attack and training before the PLAAF formed in 1949. It performs exactly like the Japanese Ko: a well-rounded fighter that climbs quickly for energy tactics and can still turn when needed, though its guns struggle against armoured bombers and attackers. It arrived in Update 1.93 "Shark Attack" as a Golden Eagles premium.
ki_84_otsu: Following the Ko into limited production, the Ki-84 Otsu replaced the mixed armament with four 20 mm Ho-5 cannons; the type had been commissioned in 1942 to succeed the Ki-43 with better guns, armour and climb, and 3,514 Ki-84s of all variants were built by the war's end. In the game the stronger guns come with the same strengths as before, excellent climb, lively performance and good handling, and the same flaws: the controls stiffen at high speed and other Japanese fighters out-turn it. It was introduced in Update 1.37.
ki_87: Built to counter B-29 raids, the Ki-87 used a turbo-supercharged Ha-44-12 radial for performance above 10,000 m, along with a pressurised cockpit and four-bladed propeller; development from 1942 was slowed by technical problems and shortages, and only one prototype flew, in April 1945. In the game it is a heavily armed super-prop whose two 30 mm and two 20 mm cannons tear bombers apart, and it is strongest high up and in dives. It turns and rolls sluggishly, overheats on WEP and benefits from manual engine control. Added as a pack in Update 1.63 "Desert Hunters", it later returned as a Golden Eagles premium.
ki_93_1_ko: Developed by the Army Aerotechnical Research Institute from 1941 and refined at the Tachikawa arsenal, the Ki-93 was a twin-engined heavy fighter and attacker with two Ha-214 radials and heavy armour around the crew. The Ko bomber-interceptor flew on 8 April 1945, was damaged landing and then destroyed in an American raid. In the game its 57 mm Ho-402 can wreck bombers with one HE hit and its APHE pierces about 70 mm of armour, while two 20 mm Ho-5s add burst mass. Steel crew plates of 12 mm, a small fuel tank and good high-altitude performance round it out. It arrived in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey".
ki_94_2: Tachikawa's Ki-94-II was a pressurised single-seat interceptor meant for high-flying B-29s, a simpler successor to the rejected twin-boom Ki-94-I, with a Ha-219 (Ha-44) engine and four wing cannons; two prototypes were built and neither flew before the war ended. In the game its strong engine, long wings and responsive elevator are offset by poor climb and slow engine response. It suits boom-and-zoom from above and hit-and-run at equal height; Spitfires out-turn it, though careful use of flaps and throttle can beat P-47s and P-51Ds. Its fuel tanks are vulnerable. It was an Operation S.U.M.M.E.R. 2017 event reward in Update 1.69.
kitsuka: Japan's first jet, Nakajima's Kikka was a Navy attack aircraft meant to hit US warships with bombs at speed; though inspired by German progress, it was a domestic design, simplified so unskilled labour could mass-produce it. Only two prototypes were tested before the war ended. In the game it is a fast fighter-bomber whose single 30 mm gains a second cannon through the 'otsu' modification. Speed is its main advantage, so heavy bomb loads of up to 800 kg are best kept for ground and naval strikes, made in fast diving runs to slip past anti-aircraft fire. It came in Update 1.43.
kor_1: The Beriev KOR-1 (later Be-2) was a two-seat, open-cockpit reconnaissance floatplane with an M-25 radial, built to replace the He 55 biplane; it was troublesome and hard to handle, only 12 were made, and they flew from shore bases rather than ships before retiring in 1942. In the game it serves as the catapult aircraft of Kirov-class cruisers and, with two nose ShKAS and one defensive ShKAS, is roughly comparable to an I-153 in firepower and handling. Two 100 kg FAB-100sv bombs give it a way to hurt coastal vessels. It was added in the "Winged Lions" update.
kor_2: Beriev's bureau designed the KOR-2 (Be-4) shipborne flying boat from 1938 because the KOR-1 handled poorly and was built too slowly. The first aircraft was finished at Savelovo in August 1941 before production moved to Omsk and, from 1944, Krasnoyarsk; they flew coastal reconnaissance, convoy escort and anti-submarine patrols in the Black Sea and were catapulted from Project 26 cruisers. In the game it is the catapult scout for Soviet ships, with a single defensive ShKAS and one forward ShKAS, but its two 100 kg bombs can threaten small boats. It came in Update 2.49 "Tusk Force".
l_39za: The L-39 Albatros was a Czechoslovak jet trainer from Letňany, developed in 1968 to replace the L-29; the L-39ZA, produced from 1980, added a reinforced wing and a ventral pod with a GSh-23L twin-barrel 23 mm cannon. Reliable, easy to maintain and able to use dirt strips, it went to more than 30 countries and many still fly. In the game it handles responsively even at top speed, has an air brake and a wide range of stores, but slow acceleration, little cannon ammunition and no ballistic computer make it hard work in air and mixed battles. It joined the Soviet tree in Update 2.47 "Leviathans".
l_39za_art_thailand: Built for the Royal Thai Air Force with Elbit electronics, the L-39ZA/ART was ordered in the early 1990s: 36 arrived by October 1993 and four more by 1997. The 401st and 411th Squadrons trained on them for fighter, attack and search-and-rescue work until the 401st switched to T-50THs in 2018 and the 411th retired its last ones in March 2021. It sits in the Japanese air tree, handling responsively with decent manoeuvrability and a useful selection of stores, but it accelerates poorly and is slow overall. It came in Update 2.57 "Heavy Cavalry".
la-11: The La-11 grew out of the La-9 as the La-130 and then La-9M, gaining fuel and weight before certification in 1947; jets made it obsolete by 1951, and after limited combat it mostly trained pilots, also serving North Korea and China. In the game the long-range La-11 is heavier than the La-9 but flies almost identically on light fuel loads, and its engine does best below about 4,000 m. Three NS-23 cannons reliably down fighters, bombers and heavy fighters. Sold as a premium pack from Update 1.65 "Way of the Samurai", it left the store after the 2018 Summer Sale and returned briefly in 2021.
la-11_china: Among the last piston fighters ever built, the La-11 was a long-range escort fighter that China's air force flew alongside the La-9 until jets arrived; it scored the PLAAF's first propeller-versus-jet kill but was also involved in shooting down a civil airliner in the mid-1950s, and survivors flew for two more decades until spares ran out. In the game it is a capable interceptor, fast and well armed enough to chase off American and British fighters, though it has one 23 mm cannon fewer than the La-9. It arrived in the "Winged Lions" update.
